<reason>B controlled the decisive weighing frame from the opening and never lost it: conceded, ongoing harms (participation tax, grammar-sorting, reward hierarchy) plus irreversible erosion versus benefits that are real but portable. A argued with more epistemic care and landed genuine friction on B's alternative — translation still needs expert judgment, translated documents are not live collaboration, and investment cannot count for B's world but be dismissed in A's. But A conceded nearly all the mechanism harms, rested its fix on admittedly nonexistent "enforceable obligations," and its coexistence examples (Germany, Japan, Finnish) all required state protection, which B converted into the debate's stickiest point: zero evidence the model works for the Quechua/Yoruba/Khmer class the motion centers. B's Q2 forced that exposure, and B's closing cleanly captured A's concessions into a single decidable question. A's "severity is not probability" partially dented the permanence frame but did not answer the harms both sides agreed are happening now. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1: flipped A's bridge metaphor into a one-way toll road, turned "complementarity" into "hierarchy with a bilingual face," converted Germany/Japan from A's shield into proof of the mechanism ("they would keep the gatekeeper and abolish the gate"), and introduced the flows-can-be-rerouted/extinctions-cannot asymmetry that structured the rest of the debate and that A never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
